lead: The action bar is the strip at the top of an activity. It shows the app icon, a title, a few action buttons and a three-dot overflow list. Those buttons are not hard-coded: they come from a menu XML file that the activity inflates, then handles by item id. This keeps commands in one resource and lets Android decide what fits. Modern apps often use a Toolbar set as the support action bar, but the menu API and item ids stay the same.
prereq: You need: 3.1, because the action bar sits above the activity's content layout.

blocks.text: An activity owns a rectangular strip at the top called the action bar. Some syllabi call the same idea the app bar. It normally contains the app icon, the activity title, action buttons that run common commands, and an overflow button drawn as three vertical dots. The overflow button opens a small list for commands that do not fit or that are rare.

Commands are declared in a menu resource, usually res/menu/main.xml. The root element is menu. Each command is an item element with android:id, android:title, android:icon and app:showAsAction. android:orderInCategory sets ordering. A group element can share visibility or checkable settings, and a nested menu element creates a submenu. The activity inflates this file at runtime; the bar is a view of the menu, not a hand-built row of buttons.

Modern code often places a Toolbar in the layout and passes it to setSupportActionBar(toolbar). The old framework action bar is then replaced by that Toolbar, but the menu callbacks and item ids do not change. The content layout sits below the bar, as described in 3.1.

sections.h3: Inflating a menu and handling clicks

blocks.text: onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) is called when the activity first needs the options menu. Call getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.main, menu), then return true. Returning false suppresses the menu.

onPrepareOptionsMenu(Menu menu) runs before the menu is shown each time. Use it to enable or disable an item, hide it, or change its title. Rotation destroys and recreates the activity, as covered in 3.2, so the menu is inflated again and prepared again.

onOptionsItemSelected(MenuItem item) receives the click. Read item.getItemId(), compare with R.id.search and other ids, run the command, and return true. Returning false makes the system fall through, so the item looks dead. The Up arrow arrives here with id android.R.id.home. Up moves up the app's screen hierarchy; the system Back button pops the back stack. They are not the same action.

showAsAction controls placement. There are three placement values. always asks for a bar slot. ifRoom takes a slot only when one is free. never keeps the item in overflow. withText is not a placement value; it is a flag joined with a pipe, for example app:showAsAction="ifRoom|withText". It shows the title beside the icon when the item is shown on the bar. Combine withText with always or ifRoom. Items marked ifRoom are placed in declaration order until the slots run out. On a Toolbar write app:showAsAction with the app namespace; the android: form is ignored.

A context menu belongs to one view, not to the whole screen. Call registerForContextMenu(view) for that view. A long press then calls onCreateContextMenu(ContextMenu menu, View v, ContextMenu.ContextMenuInfo info). Inflate the menu there and call super first. The click arrives in onContextItemSelected(MenuItem item); handle the id and return true.
Use a context menu for actions on one row or one image, such as Rename or Delete on a list item. The menu should be short. A long list belongs in a dialog or a new screen.

A PopupMenu is a floating list anchored to a view. Create it with new PopupMenu(this, anchorView), inflate its menu, set setOnMenuItemClickListener, then call show(). It is local to that anchor and does not use onCreateOptionsMenu or onOptionsItemSelected. Use it for a small choice beside a button, such as Sort by date or Sort by name.
Choose by scope: options menu for screen-wide frequent commands, context menu for one item, popup menu for a local choice. All three use the same menu XML format and item ids.

figure.caption: Search (always) takes slot 1, Share and Edit (ifRoom) take slots 2 and 3, and Delete finds no free slot. Delete and Settings (never) go to the overflow list: 3 items on the bar, 2 in overflow.

spec.aria: Five menu items listed with their showAsAction values; arrows send Search, Share and Edit to three slots on a toolbar, and Delete and Settings to the overflow list under the three-dot button.

examples.question: A Toolbar has room for 3 action slots. Its menu XML has five items: Search with showAsAction=always; Share, Edit and Delete with showAsAction=ifRoom; Settings with showAsAction=never. Which items appear on the bar, and how many go to overflow?
steps: Start with 3 free slots, an empty bar and an empty overflow list.
Search is always, so it takes slot 1. The bar is Search. Free slots are now 2.
Share is ifRoom, so it takes slot 2. The bar is Search, Share. Free slots are now 1.
Edit is ifRoom, so it takes slot 3. The bar is Search, Share, Edit. Free slots are now 0.
Delete is ifRoom, but no free slot remains, so it goes to overflow. Overflow is Delete.
Settings is never, so it goes to overflow. Overflow is Delete, Settings.
examples.answer: The bar shows 3 items, Search, Share and Edit; overflow holds 2 items, Delete and Settings.

traps: showAsAction is a custom attribute on a Toolbar, so write app:showAsAction and declare the app namespace. android:showAsAction is ignored and every item drops into overflow.
Returning false from onOptionsItemSelected lets the event fall through. The click appears to do nothing; return true after handling your id.
Up is not Back. android.R.id.home should move up the app's screen hierarchy; the system Back button pops the back stack.

In onCreateContextMenu call super first, then inflate the menu with getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.x, menu). An empty long-press menu is caused by not inflating the menu; the default super call does nothing, so a missing super alone does not empty it.
A PopupMenu uses setOnMenuItemClickListener, not onOptionsItemSelected. Mixing them leaves the popup click unhandled.

quiz.q: Which method inflates the options menu, and what should it return?
quiz.a: onCreateOptionsMenu(Menu menu) inflates with getMenuInflater().inflate(R.menu.main, menu) and returns true.

quiz.q: Name the three showAsAction placement values. What does withText do, and how is it written?
quiz.a: Placement values: always, ifRoom and never. withText is a flag joined with a pipe, for example app:showAsAction="ifRoom|withText"; it shows the title beside the icon when the item is on the bar. Combine withText with always or ifRoom.

quiz.q: Why should onOptionsItemSelected return true after handling an item?
quiz.a: True tells the system the click was consumed. Returning false lets the event fall through, so the command looks dead.

quiz.q: A menu has room for 2 slots: Home is always, Profile and Help are ifRoom, About is never. Which items are on the bar and which are in overflow?
quiz.a: Home takes slot 1. Profile takes slot 2. No free slot remains, so Help goes to overflow. About is never, so it also goes to overflow. Bar: Home and Profile. Overflow: Help and About.

quiz.q: A developer writes android:showAsAction=always on a Toolbar item. It appears only in overflow. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: showAsAction is a custom attribute. On a Toolbar the android: namespace form is ignored. Use app:showAsAction and declare the app namespace in the layout or menu file.

quiz.q: State one difference between the Up arrow and the system Back button.
quiz.a: Up moves up the app's screen hierarchy and arrives as android.R.id.home. Back pops the back stack and may leave the app.

quiz.q: A long-press menu appears but a click on its item does nothing. Which two methods should you inspect?
quiz.a: Check onCreateContextMenu to confirm the menu is inflated and super is called. Check onContextItemSelected to confirm the item id is handled and true is returned.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern Android code often uses MaterialToolbar with a menu provider so fragments can own their own menus. Selection UIs use ActionMode, a temporary bar for acting on chosen items. Search next: MenuProvider, ActionMode and MaterialToolbar. These keep the same menu XML idea but move ownership away from the activity.
